notes: Core change is the same as the reference; a dedicated segment-level table test covers heredoc, nested blocks, snippet import via `doImport`, and a quoted brace failing to close a block, but it skips the minor address-suffix and quoted `"{}"` tweaks.

Same core fix as the reference via Token methods (it also misses the minor HasSuffix and quoted "{}" tweaks); its new table test checks the actual tokens in each segment, plus snippet import, nested blocks, heredoc, and an error when a quoted brace is used to close a block.

Matches the reference: method-style helpers check `wasQuoted == 0` at every brace site in the dispenser and parser, with dispenser, parser and issue-exact adapt tests; it misses only the reference's quoted-address `HasSuffix` and quoted `"{}"` tweaks.

Same clean Token-method fix (minor HasSuffix and quoted "{}" cases unaddressed), with thorough dispenser and parser tests plus an end-to-end caddyfile adapt test that reproduces the issue's respond "{" case.

Correct fix that adds an extra layer of Dispenser wrapper methods on top of the Token helpers; one new test asserts that a quoted `"{"` address errors via the `HasSuffix` check, which the reference deliberately relaxes.

Fix is functionally equivalent to the reference but adds redundant Dispenser wrapper methods over the Token methods; tests cover dispenser and parser behavior, including a quoted '}' that does not open a block and an error case.

Same root-cause fix as the reference, using `!t.Quoted()` helpers; tests cover quoted, backtick and heredoc braces, nested blocks and an unterminated block, but it omits the minor address-suffix and quoted `"{}"` adjustments.

Adds unquoted-brace helpers on Token and uses them at every structural brace check in the dispenser and parser, matching the reference except the quoted-suffix address check and the quoted "{}" branch; tests cover quoted braces in dispenser blocks, parse cases including backtick and heredoc, and an unclosed-block error.

Recursive parent-chain slug resolution that closely mirrors the reference and handles DisablePathToLower explicitly; path.Join may silently clean unusual slugs, and the tests cover nested slugs under a non-section directory plus taxonomy/term.

A recursive slug-aware directory builder, structurally closest to the reference, that handles unnormalized paths explicitly and sets Dir only when a slug exists; path.Join may silently clean odd slugs, and the test covers a nested slug with no intermediate _index.

Uses the same segment-replacement approach as C1 but wraps it in tidy descriptor helpers with a path-boundary check; its test is the most thorough, covering bundle resources, regular pages, slugs under non-section intermediate directories, and taxonomy/term.

Same approach as C3 but tidier, with descriptor helper methods and a path-boundary check on the prefix cut; it has the most thorough test, including bundle resources, deep nested slugs and regular pages.

Computes a slug-applied Dir for every page in hugolib and uses it in CreateTargetPaths, close to the reference design; tests cover nested section slugs, a non-section subfolder, and taxonomy/term slugs.

Walks up from the current section and replaces path segments by position, which matches the reference for nested slugs, directories without an _index file, and taxonomy/term pages; the test covers nested section slugs and an intermediate directory with no section.

Replaces section path segments with ancestor slugs by index, which is correct for sections, terms and descendant pages; however, the 'empty SectionBase means no slug' convention and the prefix-splicing in CreateTargetPaths are a bit indirect, and the tests never cover slugs at more than one nesting level.
Correct via a SectionBase field plus a CutPrefix rewrite inside CreateTargetPaths, but the logic is split across two packages and the test does not exercise multi-level or deeper nested slugs.

Changes the return type to a Map of slices, which fixes the same-module case. The table-driven plan tests are good (for_each, count, a for_each import mixed with a static one, child module). Cross-module overrides still discard a child's imports of other instances, rather than deduplicating at instance level after expansion as the reference does.

Fixes the reported root-module case by grouping statements per ConfigResource, but parent-over-child override still applies to the whole resource rather than per instance, so a parent import of one instance silently drops the child's imports of other instances (the same silent-drop failure as the issue, and the cause of 2/3 hidden failures); the plan tests cover for_each, count, mixed for_each import and child-module cases well.

Fixes the reported case: same-module blocks are kept as a slice, which matches the reference caller. However, parent override still works per ConfigResource rather than per instance, so a child-module import of a different instance is still silently dropped when the parent imports one instance (1/3 hidden tests).

Returns an ordered slice, close to the reference's shape, and fixes the root-module for_each case, but keeps resource-level parent override instead of instance-level dedup at expansion time, so child-module imports can still be silently dropped; tests are a single root plan test plus a unit test whose override case uses only a single-instance resource.

Same slice-plus-owner-map approach as C1, plus a defensive full-slice fix for append aliasing. It keeps resource-level parent override, and its unit test explicitly asserts that the child's c["y"] import is dropped, locking in the remaining silent-drop bug.

Slice-based approach with a module-owner map plus a harmless defensive fix for slice aliasing, but it has the same resource-level override flaw; its unit test asserts that child-y is dropped, and the plan test only covers a two-instance root case.

Code is essentially identical to C3 (Map of slices, resource-level parent override). It has solid integration tests, but its unit test explicitly encodes dropping the child's baz["q"] import, the same class of silent loss the issue complains about.

Same code as C1, with the same resource-level override flaw that silently discards child imports for other instances; its new unit test explicitly asserts that the child's baz["q"] import is dropped, locking in the wrong behavior.

It works and has tests at both the executor and consolidation level, but it puts CLI-specific '--once' semantics and error messages into the public lib/executor package, dereferences cmd unconditionally, and misses the lower-layer shortcut case.

It works and has good consolidation and unit tests, but a CLI-specific '--once' function and error message are pushed into the exported lib/executor API, and env shortcuts that wipe script scenarios are not handled.

The applyOnce implementation is solid, and the unit and end-to-end tests are excellent (they verify setup/teardown, env and tags at runtime), but it adds unrelated proxy-unsetting TestMain hooks in two test packages and misses the lower-layer shortcut case.

The post-consolidation rewrite is clean and handles the 0/1/many scenario cases and CLI conflicts, but it does not drop env/config shortcuts that clear script scenarios, ignores execution-segment, and adds unrelated proxy-unsetting TestMain hacks in two test files.

The once.go implementation is clean and correct, with validation before CLI parsing and post-consolidation rewriting, but it does not handle env/config shortcuts that drop script scenarios before the rewrite, and it edits an unrelated stdlog integration test (removing the hosts option) as an environment workaround.

The dedicated once.go is tidy and clones env/tags, though it validates flags redundantly, and it rewrites an unrelated existing stdlog integration test to dodge a sandbox proxy, which is an out-of-scope change to test semantics.

It carries Once through every CLI config getter (run, cloud local, partial) and rewrites inside getConsolidatedConfig with focused consolidation tests and no unrelated changes, but, like the others, it misses lower-layer shortcuts that silently drop the script's scenario.

Carrying Once on Config and applying it inside getConsolidatedConfig closely mirrors the reference design and covers run, cloud and archive with focused consolidation tests, but it lacks the reference's lower-layer shortcut dropping and execution-segment checks.

Round-trip works and it has thorough tests including parse-time error cases, but it leaves DurationExpr.Pretty printing `+5` for the new wrapper, repeats the wrap logic in the grammar, and adds an inconsistent experimental-flag guard only on the offset unary rule.

It wraps bare literals in a Wrapped unary-plus DurationExpr in both paren rules and keeps the parse-time 'duration must be greater than 0' check, including for -(5); but it leaves DurationExpr.Pretty unchanged (so it would print '(+5)'), gates only one rule on the experimental flag, and repeats the wrapping logic in the grammar instead of applyUnaryOpToDurationExpr.

Fixes String() round-trip and keeps parse-time positive checks including negation, but omits the Pretty() unary-plus fix, repeats the wrap logic in the grammar, and uses an unconditional `$2.(*NumberLiteral)` assertion.

Wrapping works and the positions (paren start/end) match the reference, but Pretty is not updated, paren_duration_expr uses an unchecked $2.(*NumberLiteral) assertion that panics if any other Expr appears there, and the positive-duration check was rewritten without any test covering it.

Cleanest and closest to the reference (generic wrap helper, unary path wraps first, Pretty updated), with solid round-trip, AST and evaluation tests, but like the reference it moves the zero/negative range check from parse time to eval time.

Closely matches the reference, using one wrapDurationExpr helper in both paren_duration_expr and applyUnaryOpToDurationExpr and updating Pretty to drop unary plus; the only nit is that the wrapper's StartPos is the inner literal rather than the paren, and tests cover offset, range, subquery and eval cases.

Matches the reference approach: a generic wrapDurationExpr is used in both the paren rule and applyUnaryOpToDurationExpr, Pretty is updated, and the positive_duration_expr check looks through the ADD wrapper so `foo[(0s)]` still fails at parse time, though `foo[-(5)]` is no longer caught there.

Same clean helper-based approach as the reference, with the Pretty update, plus an unwrap helper so positive_duration_expr still rejects foo[(0s)] at parse time, backed by a test; the change is focused and well tested.

Follows the reference structure (`walkTemplateOld` rename, fork script, error for valued returns outside partials). However, `moveReturnLast` only relocates `return` when the next arg is a bare identifier, which breaks common forms like `return resources.Get "x"` and `return .Site.GetPage "p"`. It also duplicates the `walkTemplate` body and swallows valued returns inside nested templates.

Close to the reference structurally (error-based partial value, non-partial valued-return error, fork script rename), but `moveReturnLast` only treats bare identifiers as functions, so common forms like `return strings.ToUpper .` or `return .Resources.GetMatch "x"` now error, and valued returns are swallowed at `{{ template }}` boundaries.

The sentinel-plus-context design works for early returns. However, `walkTemplate` swallows every return, so a valued `{{ return }}` inside a `{{ template }}` called from a partial is silently lost. `exec.go` is edited directly without updating the fork script, and a trailing pipe after `return` is silently dropped.

Similar context-pointer design with good isolation for nested executions, but valued returns are swallowed at `{{ template }}` boundaries, `return x | f` silently drops `f`, and exec.go is edited without updating the fork script, so the change would be lost on re-fork.

Similar to C1, but it updates the fork script (via a somewhat fragile string replacement) and handles `return X | f` pipelines sensibly. It still swallows valued returns at `{{ template }}` boundaries, which likely causes the hidden-test failure.

The sentinel-error approach via context works in any position, and wrapping the whole pipeline into the return argument is a nice touch; however, the walkTemplate boundary swallows valued returns, so `{{ template }}` inside a partial loses the value (likely the failing hidden test), and the fork-script replacer depends on an exact source string.

A clean `ErrReturn` sentinel and a context-stored value pass every hidden test, and valued returns reach the enclosing partial even through `{{ template }}`. Weaknesses: the context value is never cleared, so nested executions such as shortcodes via `.Content` or `ExecuteAsTemplate` can leak into the outer partial. `exec.go` is edited without a fork-script update, and valued returns in non-partials are silently ignored.

A simple `ErrReturn` sentinel with the value stored via ctx passes all tests, including valued returns through `{{ template }}`; it is leaky (nested executions sharing ctx can set the partial's value, `return x | f` silently drops `f`, valued returns in non-partials are ignored) and edits exec.go without a fork-script replacer.
